Speed
SPEED
n. & v.
From Anglo-Saxon sped, success, prosperity, good fortune — the sense of swiftness is later. Webster 1828: success; prosperity in an undertaking; hence the old greeting God speed, a wish for God’s prosperity upon a man’s way.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version preserves the older meaning, in which speed is success rather than swiftness. Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, prays for it by name: O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham (Genesis 24:12). He is asking for prosperity in the errand, and the chapter is one of the clearest narratives of ordinary providence in Scripture — the answer arrives before he has finished speaking. The word’s most weighty use is a prohibition. John forbids the church to pronounce that blessing over a false teacher: If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed (2 John 1:10), and he gives the reason in the next breath: he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds (2 John 1:11). To wish a man success is to take a share in what he is doing. The apostle of love writes this, and it is not an inconsistency; love for the flock requires that its enemies not be sped on their way with a blessing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPEED as success; prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; and secondarily swiftness, quickness, celerity. The phrase God speed is a wish for prosperity upon a man’s undertaking.

expand to see more

SPEED, n. — Success; prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; as, to bid one good speed.

Swiftness; quickness; celerity; haste; dispatch.

SPEED, v.i. — To make haste; to move with celerity; also, to have success; to prosper.

SPEED, v.t. — To dispatch; to send away in haste; to hasten; also, to prosper; to cause to succeed.

Anglo-Saxon sped, success, from spedan, to prosper — the sense of swiftness is secondary and later.

Key Scripture

Genesis 24:12 — "And he said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham."

2 John 1:10 — "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:"

2 John 1:11 — "For he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds."

Genesis 24:27 — "And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren."

Modern Corruption

2 John 1:10-11 forbids extending the church’s blessing to a teacher who denies the doctrine of Christ, and the modern reflex to call every such refusal unloving has the apostle of love against it.

expand to see more

The instruction is precise and it is limited. John is not addressing personal rudeness toward unbelievers, nor secondary disagreements among brethren; the doctrine of Christ in view is the incarnation itself, denied by the deceivers of verse 7 who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. Against that specific denial the church is told to withhold hospitality and greeting, on the stated ground that a blessing makes the blesser a partaker. This cuts directly against the ecumenical instinct that treats joint platforms and public warmth as costless expressions of charity. They are not costless; John says they transfer a share in the deeds. The 1689 Confession’s chapter on the church assumes exactly this discipline, and the Reformers’ refusal to grant Rome’s gospel a place alongside their own was an application of it, not an excess of zeal.

The opposite abuse must be named too, because this text has been used to justify separation from brethren over matters John was not discussing. The doctrine of Christ is the boundary here — not the millennial position, not the mode of church government, not every difference on which a faithful man may err. To wield 2 John against the confessionally orthodox is to make a rule for heretics do work against brothers, and it produces the sectarianism that has repeatedly fractured otherwise sound churches. Genesis 24 supplies the positive picture the word was made for: a servant asking God for good speed in a lawful errand, and receiving it before he had done speaking.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qarah (H7136), to cause to meet or occur favourably; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice, used as a greeting; the KJV phrase God speed renders the ordinary Greek salutation.

expand to see more

Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to cause to occur, to bring about a meeting; send me good speed this day (Genesis 24:12).

Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, and as a greeting hail; the word behind God speed in 2 John 1:10-11.

Greek koinoneo (G2841) — to share in, to be partaker of; the consequence John attaches to the greeting (2 John 1:11).

Anglo-Saxon sped — success, prosperity; the original English sense preserved in the Authorized Version.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper, to succeed; the standing Old Testament word for a prospered way.

Usage

"Send me good speed this day (Genesis 24:12) — a prayer for success in an errand, answered before he had finished speaking."

"Neither bid him God speed (2 John 1:10) — the church’s blessing withheld from a denier of the incarnation."

"He that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds (2 John 1:11) — a blessing transfers a share."
